mainEntity.name: How much does a Mercedes S63 AMG engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A rebuilt M157 engine for the S63 costs £7,000-£10,000 supply-only; a rebuilt M177 engine costs £8,000-£12,000 supply-only. Fitting adds £1,500-£2,500 depending on complexity - AMG V8 work requires specialist knowledge.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of oil separator failure on a Mercedes S63 AMG (M177)?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most common sign is a burning oil smell or oil dripping from the rear of the engine. A whistling noise or rough idle can also be early indicators. If ignored, oil separator failure leads to rear main seal leaks and potentially bottom-end damage.

mainEntity.name: Is the Mercedes S63 AMG V8 engine (M177/M157) reliable?

acceptedAnswer.text: The M157 and M177 are fundamentally strong hand-built AMG V8s - some of Mercedes' most impressive modern engines. The M157 has known timing chain and oil consumption issues, while the M177 suffers from oil separator, rear main seal, intercooler leak, and oil pump wiring harness (P06DA00) problems. With proper maintenance and early intervention on known issues, these engines routinely exceed 100,000 miles.

mainEntity.name: How long does a Mercedes S63 AMG engine last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Properly maintained M157 V8 engines routinely reach 100,000-150,000 miles before major work, though timing chain and oil consumption issues can occur from 40,000 miles. The M177 is too new for definitive long-term data, but with proactive maintenance on known issues, 100,000+ miles is achievable.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in my Mercedes S63 AMG?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if the S63 is otherwise in good condition with no rust or major electrical faults. A rebuilt M157 costs £7,000-£10,000 - far less than replacing a £20,000-£45,000 vehicle. The M177's higher value (£45,000-£85,000) makes replacement even more financially justifiable.

mainEntity.name: What oil does my Mercedes S63 AMG need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mercedes-Benz specifies MB 229.5 high-performance oil - typically 5W-30 or 5W-40 fully synthetic. The M157 V8 requires approximately 9.5 litres; the M177 V8 requires approximately 9.5 litres.

historyTimeline.h2: Mercedes Benz S Class S63 - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The S63 AMG has represented the pinnacle of Mercedes performance luxury since its debut in the W221 generation in 2011, powered by the M157 5.5-litre twin-turbo V8 delivering 544-585hp. In 2014, the W222 S63 continued with the M157, producing 585hp. The 2018 W222 facelift introduced the M177 4.0-litre twin-turbo V8 with 612hp and 900Nm of torque, featuring the AMG Speedshift MCT 9-speed transmission. This hand-built engine from Affalterbach represents the pinnacle of AMG V8 engineering.

milestones.description: M157.980, 5.5L twin-turbo V8, 544hp @ 5,500rpm (S63 AMG, W221 launch)
2021 - M177.980, 4.0L twin-turbo V8, 612hp @ 5,500rpm (S63 AMG 4MATIC+, W222 facelift)

commonProblems.h2: Mercedes Benz S Class S63 Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The S63's M157 and M177 hand-built V8s represent the pinnacle of AMG engineering - powerful, refined, and coveted by enthusiasts. However, both have well-documented weaknesses that can lead to significant repair costs. The M157 suffers from timing chain tensioner wear and oil consumption issues, while the M177 is prone to oil separator failure, rear main seal leaks, intercooler coolant leaks, and oil pump wiring harness failure (P06DA00). Every rebuilt engine supplied through EnginesMarket includes upgraded components addressing these original failure points, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited-mileage warranty.

problems.group: M177 Oil Separator Failure & Rear Main Seal Leak
problems.h4: M177 Oil Separator Failure & Rear Main Seal Leak - The Most Expensive M177 Problem
problems.rootCause: The PCV oil separator diaphragm fails, allowing excessive crankcase vacuum that pulls the rear main seal inward, resulting in a massive oil leak. This is a known issue on M177-powered vehicles. Mercedes-Benz mandates that both oil separators be replaced whenever a rear main seal is found leaking. One owner reported a $7,000 USD repair for the rear main seal and oil separators on a 2019 S63.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Diagnostic scan, crankcase pressure test, inspect oil separators
repairOptions.longevity: Confirms whether separator or seal is the root cause

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace both oil separators (PCV valves), inspect crankcase ventilation system
repairOptions.longevity: If caught before seal damage occurs

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace rear main seal, drop transmission, inspect flywheel
repairOptions.longevity: If seal has failed but no bottom-end damage

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete engine swap with upgraded oil separators and rear main seal, 12-month warranty
repairOptions.longevity: If oil loss has caused bearing or bottom-end damage

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical 2018-2021 S63 AMG 4MATIC+ is worth approximately £45,000-£85,000 depending on mileage and condition. The S63 sits firmly in the £15,000+ band - replacement cost is typically small relative to vehicle value, making a full rebuilt engine a justifiable investment for owners of these high-value performance flagships.
problems.recommendation: The oil separator is the root cause of most M177 rear main seal leaks. If you notice oil around the transmission bellhousing, a burning oil smell, or hear a whistling noise from the engine, have the crankcase pressure checked immediately. If caught early, replacing the oil separators alone (£1,000-£1,600 at a specialist) prevents the much more expensive rear main seal replacement. If the rear main seal has already failed, replacing both the seal and the oil separators together is the only sensible approach. On an S63 worth £45,000-£85,000, the full rebuilt engine route is justifiable if bottom-end damage has occurred.

problems.h4: M177 Intercooler Coolant Leaks - The Hot-Vee V8's Hidden Danger
problems.rootCause: The engine-mounted water-to-air intercoolers on the M177 can develop internal leaks, allowing coolant to enter the intake tract. This is a critical failure - coolant ingestion can cause catastrophic engine damage and hydrolock. Symptoms include unexplained coolant loss in the low-temp circuit, engine misfires (P0300-P0308), and white, sweet-smelling exhaust smoke.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Pressure test intercooler system to confirm leak location
repairOptions.longevity: Essential before committing to any repair

repairOptions.longevity: If coolant leak has caused engine damage

problems.vehicleValueCheck: As above - a typical S63 is worth £45,000-£85,000.
problems.recommendation: Intercooler leaks on the M177 are a known and potentially catastrophic issue. If you experience coolant loss without an obvious external leak, or if you notice misfires, have the intercooler system pressure tested immediately. Do not drive with a suspected internal intercooler leak - it risks catastrophic engine damage from coolant ingestion and hydrolock. Specialist pricing for intercooler replacement is significantly lower than dealer rates. If one intercooler has failed, consider replacing both - the other will typically fail within a similar timeframe due to shared operating conditions.

problems.group: M177 Oil Pump Wiring Harness Failure (P06DA00)
problems.h4: M177 Oil Pump Wiring Harness Failure (P06DA00) - The Electronic Oil Pressure Fault
problems.rootCause: The M177's electronically controlled variable pressure oil pump suffers from a common electronic failure, not mechanical. Fault code P06DA00 is caused by a brittle wiring harness inside the oil pan. Replacement is a massive job requiring the engine and transmission to be removed from the vehicle, with labour costs often exceeding £5,000.

repairOptions.longevity: Confirms whether pump or wiring is the cause

problems.vehicleValueCheck: As above - a typical S63 is worth £45,000-£85,000.
problems.recommendation: If your S63 displays fault code P06DA00, do not delay. The pump defaults to maximum pressure in a 'safe' mode, which prevents immediate engine damage but keeps the check engine light on. However, if you see a low oil pressure warning or hear engine knocking, do not drive the vehicle. Specialist oil pump wiring harness replacement at £3,500-£5,500 is significantly cheaper than dealer rates, though it remains an engine-out job. On an S63 worth £45,000-£85,000, this is a justifiable investment.
